Agidigbo（又稱molo）是奈及利亞約魯巴人使用的撥奏式舌簧琴，屬H-S: The agidigbo (also called molo) is a plucked lamellophone of the Yoruba of Nigeria, H-S 122.1. Its body is a box that can rest on the knee, with four or five metal lamellae side by side on the top surface, bent so that they vibrate and sound. The player plucks one or two rhythm lamellae with the left hand and three melodic lamellae with the right, and may also strike the side with a thick ring or tap the top with the thumb or knuckles. It is common in apala music.

演奏者可坐姿將琴箱置於腿上，或以繩掛於頸部、懸於腰間。發聲以手指彈撥箱面金屬簧片: The player sits with the box on the legs, or hangs it from the neck by a cord at waist height. It sounds when the fingers pluck the metal lamellae on the box face: the left hand takes one or two rhythm lamellae and the right hand three melodic ones, and a skilled player uses as many fingers as possible. A thick ring may also strike the wooden side, or the thumb and knuckles tap the face. A beginner first learns the division between the hands and the high and low placing of the lamellae, then practises the tapped sounds.

阿吉迪格博主要出現在約魯巴的阿帕拉音樂中，也可為塞凱雷、瓦卡或阿帕拉樂團伴奏。二: The agidigbo appears mainly in Yoruba apala music and can also accompany sẹkẹrẹ, waka or apala ensembles. Before the 1920s it was used in indigenous music; it later entered apala with the new popular forms and is most widespread in the Ibadan and Ijebu areas. For listening, hear Babatunde Olatunji's playing on track seven of his 1959 album Drums of Passion, “Oyin Momo Ado” (sweet as honey).
阿吉迪格博以金屬簧片振動發聲，音色宏亮。三片旋律簧片相鄰音程為二度或三度，最低與: The agidigbo sounds from the vibration of metal lamellae and is loud. The three melodic lamellae are a second or a third apart, and the lowest and highest lie no more than a fifth apart; the two rhythm lamellae have only a relative high and low. The player plucks with the fingers and adds percussive sound by striking the side with a thick ring or tapping the face with the thumb or knuckles. The source does not describe any means of controlling volume, nor how it differs from related instruments.
阿吉迪格博又稱 molo，為奈及利亞約魯巴人的傳統彈撥式拇指琴，早期用於本土音樂: The agidigbo, also called molo, is a traditional plucked thumb piano of the Yoruba of Nigeria; it was used in indigenous music and was still in use in the 1920s. As new popular music arose, musicians brought its sound and playing into apala, and it is most widespread in the Ibadan and Ijebu areas of Yorubaland. It can accompany sẹkẹrẹ, waka or apala ensembles; the seventh track of a 1959 album, “Oyin Momo Ado”, also uses it.

The sounding bodies are definitely metal, and the body can be confirmed to include wooden parts. As for the rest of the box, the hanging cord and the accessories such as the thick ring used in playing, the source gives no materials and none are guessed at.
